units.text: Of lakes and knowledges: between disciplinary enclosures and the pursuit of "full transdisciplinarity"
Introduction

Despite the long-standing recognition of the need for enhanced interdisciplinary coordination to tackle the global challenges we face in relation to the farreaching socio-natural transformations of our planet, notably the anthropogenic alterations of the hydrosphere, the production of knowledge and its application to policy design and implementation oriented at addressing these challenges, only seldom constitute satisfying examples of such type of coordination.In fact, the vast literature on inter and transdisciplinarity published in the last two decades strongly suggests that, in practice, we are still far from achieving the degrees of progress expected or predicted since at least the 1960s.The main objective of the article is to revisit key aspects of the long-standing debates on the challenges of interdisciplinary research, placing emphasis on water-related, including lakes, research.In the first section I position myself as a sociologist experiencing some of these challenges.The second and third sections examine different aspects of the long-standing debates about the obstacles and prospects of interdisciplinary research, and the notions of inter and transdisciplinarity.The fourth section addresses some relevant examples of "x"-disciplinary research in the production of lake-related knowledge.The fifth and last section discusses the contradictions and challenges facing "x"-disciplinary water and lake-related research in the context of the current global socio-ecological mega crisis.
A sociologist in the labyrinth

This article was written from the perspective of a sociologist who, at some point in his early career, accepted the challenge to enter the "labyrinth" of acquiring knowledge about the "sublime obscurity" of Nature, borrowing from d'Alembert's observation on the paradox of the diversity and unity of the sciences (d'Alembert 2011(d'Alembert [1751]]:17).I explain this here because, as argued by several authors, to a significant extent, Sociology, particularly during much of the twentieth century, was developed as "if Nature did not matter" (Murphy 1995), and, to an important degree, remains so, which is also applicable to other social science disciplines like Political Science or mainstream Economics.Clearly, the converse could be stated about "harder" disciplines, that continue to develop as if, broadly speaking, social processes did not matter, could be simply taken as the background of what "really counts" in scientific research or be subordinated to the presumably higher interests of techno-scientific enterprising, whereby "softer" disciplines could at most aspire to provide "backend" fixing services, for example, by facilitating the acceptance of technocratic decisions by reluctant or suspecting would-be beneficiaries (Lowe et al. 2013).Overcoming these long-standing entrenched barriers to meaningful inter and transdisciplinary engagement continues to be a major challenge owing to a diversity of epistemic, institutional, or academic-political reasons, whose actual significance as obstacles remains open to widespread debate.Although these barriers and obstacles are largely intrinsic to scientific endeavours, as argued by some authors, external obstacles are often significant too (Shinn 2006).In this connection, the production of scientific knowledge is influenced by external systemic societal conditions that strongly weight on or even determine why and how knowledge is produced, by whom, and for whom.Perhaps one of the more instigating readings on this topic, suggested to me by the late sociologist Herminio Martins, was Loren Graham's "The Ghost of the Executed Engineer" (1993), a study of what can be defined as the shrinking of cosmopolitan, broadminded, integral approaches in the techno sciences into narrowfocused reductionist disciplinary specialization.I will revisit the significance of systemic conditions to produce knowledge at the end of the article.

Going back to water and lakes, for a long time, my involvement with lakes was limited to human curiosity and bodily experiences, whether as a tourist, an occasional fisherman or as an inquisitive resident of lacustrine regions, which gave me an enduring practical awareness of the centrality of water in what much later I came to understand as socioecological processes.In this regard, despite my frequent and diversified encounters with lakes and other water bodies, it took over a decade of later academic training as a sociologist until I started to acquire elements of what Jean Piaget termed "cognitive structures" (Piaget 1977: 342-346;1978: 43-46) that would help me to observe "water" as an object of sociological enquiry.In the course of this intellectual process of cognitive assimilation and accommodation, new opportunities to experience momentous encounters with lakes appeared in my horizon while I was undertaking postgraduate studies on urban water conflicts in one of the largest global urbanizations, the Mexico City Metropolitan Area much of which is built on the bed of a desiccated lake system with a very long-term complex history that continues to attract substantial, increasingly interdisciplinary, scholarly attention (Cordova 2022).By then I was already a trained academic observing and conceptualizing water and water-related human interactions from a sociology "as if Nature did not matter" perspective, which I started to question and refocus by trespassing boundaries and establishing meaningful dialogues and exchanges with colleagues from physical natural and technical disciplines, particularly hydrology, physical geography, and civil engineering, many of whom were expanding their intellectual and professional research interests to embrace topics as the history and archaeology of hydraulic infrastructure but were also concerned with the sociology of water politics (Cabrera and Arregui 2010).Moving along these bifurcations I came to experience again meaningful encounters with lakes, while engaging in interdisciplinary research projects with a team of Finnish engineers natural from a land and culture very rich in lakes, and lakesloving people Juuti and Katko (2005), Katko (2016), Katko et al. (2001Katko et al. ( -2004)), Katko et al. (2016).In addition, my expanding web of engagements beyond my disciplinary harbour came to include interactions with representatives of water-related organizations, as well as lasting connections with wider publics pertinent to my research, like farmers, members of basin committees, urban water users, and social movements committed to political struggles in defence of water as a common or public good, among others.Unsurprisingly, the trespassing of disciplinary boundaries and the testing of institutional elasticities attracted reactions, like cautionary messages asking me to renounce "undisciplined" social science approaches, reactions perhaps aimed at bringing me back into a presumably safer, less adventurous, "orderly" and more restrained career path.With hindsight, those offputting remarks provided constructive lessons, and reinforced my conviction about the imperative need to transcend disciplinary boundaries and enclosures to better understand and produce meaningful knowledge about socioecological processes, including those that are water-related (Castro 2010), Swyngedouw (1996, 2004).Nonetheless, perhaps the richest intellectual experience has been to re-read the social science classics, who actually, despite much dismissive uproar to the contrary did provide a legacy of insightful foundations to address socio-ecological processes in holistic and more integrated perspectives (Dunlap et al. 2002), before disciplinarization and specialization narrowed down the scope and restricted the array of research objects deemed worthy, proper or feasible for sociological undertakings, reductionist processes which include what Norbert Elias called "the retreat of sociologists into the present", referring to the trend to recoil from long-term historical analyses and restrict the temporal dimension of sociological research to conjunctural situations, that gained traction among many twentieth century sociologists (Martins 1974;Goudsblom 1977;Elias 1978Elias , 1994Elias , 2009;;De Vries and Goudsblom 2002).Retrospectively, this sociologist is still trapped in d'Alembert's labyrinth of "sublime obscurity", but glad that the labyrinth is well populated.
Knowledge labyrinths and "x"-disciplinarities

A revision of even a small sample of the considerable literature on the challenges posed by the puzzling interlinkages between the unity and diversity of the sciences (few examples are Weingart and Stehr 2000;Nowotny et al. 2001;Max-Neef 2005;Sawyer 2005;Kagan 2009;Bhaskar et al. 2010;Nicolescu 2012;Lowe et al. 2013;Brandt et al. 2013;Bammer 2014;Bernstein 2015;Scholz and Steiner 2015;Krueger et al. 2016;Boon and van Baalen 2019) brings up to date d'Alembert's labyrinth metaphor.However even a succinct historical review of these debates, taking the early 1970s as a reference point, insinuates the unsettling inference that the progress made over the last few decades has been somewhat limited, while foundational contributions seem to have been neglected or, worse, are frequently reproduced as novelties in recent publications, even without adequate recognition of the sources of what is a decadesold debate.A healthy counter example of this regrettable trend, though, is the acknowledgement of the seminal character of the 1972 report "Interdisciplinarity: Problems of teaching and research in universities", which presented the results of an international seminar organized by the Organization for Economic Cooperation andDevelopment (OECD) in 1970 (Apostel et al. 1972).In the Conclusions, the editors commented:

Glancing over the foregoing pages one could get the impression that interdisciplinarity is merely a hodgepodge of elements, judging from the variety of activities which are called interdisciplinary, from the divergence or even contradiction between some of the concepts used, from the multiplicity of purposes, from the mixture of humanism and "scientism", from the coexistence of revolutionary aspirations or concern for meeting the needs of society more closely.It would be tempting to throw out the very notion that there was any unity involved and to suppose instead that it was a mere chance encounter made possible by ambiguous nomen-clature.Above all, one might adopt a normative attitude, thinking in terms of hierarchies, and speak of "true and "false" interdisciplinarity distinguishing lesser or greater degrees of integration which could approximately match the list of multi-, pluri-, inter-, transdisciplinarity, or else one could set up a tight typology for the purpose of clearing up such confusion (Apostel et al. 1972: 71).

The authors eventually decided against giving up to the temptation of taking the normative path mentioned at the end of the quotation, as they recognized the difficulties involved in the heterogeneity of approaches and the lack of adequate theories to define "interdisciplinarity" in a way sufficiently convincing for all participants in that seminar.Still, the report remarked that the results reflected that, at that moment in time, "interdisciplinarity was an 'epistemologically naïve concept'", characterized by a certain "nostalgy for world unity and the hope of rediscovering the obscure universality of original experience among the fragments of science" (Apostel et al. 1972: 71-72).Despite the decades passed since the report's publication and the significant advances in scientific knowledge achieved since, to a great extent, its succinct conclusions describe the current state of the art on the subject.It is worth highlighting here also the analysis provided by one of the participants in the same seminar, Jean Piaget, who anticipated many of the arguments that are often presented in the more recent literature with apparent unawareness of the pre-existing contributions.In a chapter that is part of the report, Piaget stated:

If we wished to draw some conclusions on the nature of interdisciplinarity […] we should be prompted to distinguish three levels, […].The lower level might be called "multidisciplinary" and occurs when the solution to a problem makes it necessary to obtain information from two or more sciences or sectors of knowledge without the disciplines drawn on thereby being changed or enriched.This situation could be a first stage which would subsequently be transcended but would last a fairly long time.This is often observed when research teams are formed with an interdisciplinary objective and at first keep their discussions on the level of mutual and cumulative information but without any actual interactions.[…] We shall keep the term interdisciplinarity to designate the second level where cooperation among various disciplines or heterogeneous sectors in the same science lead to actual interactions, to a certain reciprocity of exchanges resulting in mutual enrichment […].Finally, we may hope to see a higher stage succeeding the stage of interdisciplinary relationships.This would be "transdisciplinarity" which would not only cover interactions or reciprocities between specialized research projects but would place these relationships within a total system without any firm boundaries between disciplines.While this is still a dream, it does not seem to be unattainable… (Piaget 1972: 136-139).

With hindsight, Piaget's dream has not yet been attained and we are still far from the stage that he termed "full transdisciplinarity" (Piaget 1972: 135), which he saw as the chief objective.In addition, the very attempt to develop higher integration between the sciences has become the object of distrust and criticism from different quarters and perspectives, given what some authors consider would be a potentially dangerous, extremely totalizing pretension to unify the sciences (Malaina 2014;Klenk and Meehan 2015;Popa, et al. 2015).From another perspective, the debate about "x" disciplinarity continues to be peppered by multiple prefixes and qualifiers, suggesting that the "confusion" and "ambiguous nomenclature", borrowing from the 1972 OECD report (Apostel et al. 1972: 71), has probably increased rather than been cleared up.Moreover, the discussion is strongly determined by the dominant languages in which we think and communicate in scientific circles, especially in the Western context, languages that, despite our claims of universalistic credentials, are charged with ethnocentric and nation-centric concerns and standpoints.If we broaden our vision to include non-Western scientific traditions, the complexity of this discussion increases substantially.Still, as suggested by Piaget, even if the objective to attain stages with higher levels of interdisciplinary coordination remains extremely difficult and elusive, it is not intrinsically unreachable, at least if we see it as a collective ambition, a common project of the species.
Ebbs and flows of knowledges

As mentioned earlier, the ambition to achieve a more integrated, higher level of interdisciplinary coordination has raised important objections, notably in relation with the perceived Western-centric character of many scientific discussions about this topic.In this connection, it is worth recalling here a debate triggered by Joseph Needham, the British specialist on the historical development of science in China, who proposed:

What metaphor then can we use to describe the way in which the medieval sciences of both West and East were subsumed in modern science?The sort of image which occurs most naturally to those who work in this field is that of the rivers and the sea.There is an old Chinese expression about "the Rivers going to pay court to the Sea", and indeed one can well consider the older streams of science in the different civilisations like rivers flowing into the ocean of modern science.Modern science is indeed composed of contributions from all the peoples of the Old World, and each contribution has flowed continuously into it, whether from Greek and Roman antiquity, or from the Islamic world or from the cultures of China and of India (Needham 2004: 24-25).This all-encompassing metaphor of scientific development after the image of a multi fluvial fluidity feeding a common global sea of knowledge, attracted criticisms and stimulated debates about the Western-centric character of studies about the interrelations between scientific cultures, although Needham himself had alerted against ethnocentric, and particularly Eurocentric visions of science (Dun 1999;Hart 1999;Elshakry 2010).Some of these criticisms of Needham's argument focus on central topics relevant to this article.For example, according to Brennan and Lo:

[there is] a problem with Needham's metaphor, of many rivers pouring into a single ecumenical sea of science.This is not an issue just for questions of East meets West, but also in understanding local and regional traditions and ways of knowledge, even when we confine attention to these within a single social and cultural tradition.What if there are several seas, lakes, and marshes, and what if some of the rivers are best imagined not in terms of fusion, but in terms of sharing some of their courses before separating and feeding different lakes or seas (Brennan and Norva 2016: 24)?

The alternative metaphor suggested by Brennan and Lo is a warning to avoid overgeneralizations and remain cautious when addressing the classical dilemma about the unity and diversity of the sciences, and knowledges more generally.Thus, rather than a common and convergent legacy that would have become crystalized in the vast repository inherited by "modern" science, human knowledge, including science, would be better characterized as being the result of convergent and divergent ebbs and flows, with meanders, backwaters, bifurcations, layers, and ephemeral accumulations across space and time.

In this regard, the long-term historical development of scientific knowledge, was subject to the new bifurcations and ramifications produced through the processes of specialization and disciplinarization that occurred since the nineteenth century, which, by the late twentieth century, had created an estimated nine thousand different fields of knowledge (Weingart and Stehr 2000).However, in retrospective, the emergence of new fields of knowledge and disciplines was not a result of mechanical processes of bifurcation and isolation, as could be thought from an overgeneralization of Needham's metaphor.Instead, borrowing again from d'Alembert's reflections (op cit.), it resulted from enduring interrelations, interconnections, and interdependencies existing between the different fields.As put by Rolando García,

The new disciplines co-emerged through an alternation of differentiation and integration processes.Thus, disciplines coevolved in an articulated manner, and the forms of articulation also evolved, in response to inner developments in each discipline (García 2006: 26-27, italics in the original).

Generically, this view of the historic-genetic character of the differentiation and integration undercurrents accounting for disciplinarization and specialization processes is shared by other authors.For example, Mittelstrass argued: it is advisable to remind oneself that subjects and disciplines have grown through the history of science, and that their boundaries are thus determined neither by their objects themselves, nor by theory, but by historical growth.Furthermore, their identity is determined by certain objects of research, theories, methods, aims of research, which often do not correspond univocally to the definitions of subjects or disciplines, but which instead overlap these disciplines (Mittelstrass 2011: 330).

Mittelstrass also illustrated how historically the objects of knowledge were often not clearly fit to their nominal disciplines, that is, objects have often been not just "undisciplined" but have even changed discipline over time, for example owing to theoretical advances and reformulations, as it happened with heat, historically an object of Physics, that in the eighteenth century became an object of Chemistry, and then, owing to newer scientific advances in the nineteenth century, came back to its ancient locus as an object of Physics (Mittelstrass 2011: 330).

Thinking about water and lakes as objects of knowledge after these considerations recalls the labyrinthic image of simultaneous enclosure and seemingly endless bifurcated fluidities, and prompts some questions:

Is it possible to clearly identify disciplines or fields of knowledge that could legitimately claim to have epistemological primacy in water-related studies?Where does water fit as a primary object of study?Is it Physics?Chemistry?Biology?Or rather Hydrology or techno-scientific branches like Hydraulic Engineering?Can we study water as if socio-natural processes did not matter?What role play the Social Sciences, the Humanities, History, Law, or Health?These are open-ended interrogations, and inevitably so, because of the continuous ebbs and flows and new ramifications of knowledges about water, which increasingly include contributions from emergent side streams like spatial archaeology (Harrower 2016), computational environmental ethnography (Entwistle et al. 2013), astrobiology, exobiology, or molecular chemical engineering (Pohorille and Pratt 2012), just to mention a few examples.It seems that Jerome Kagan's book "The Three Cultures.Natural Sciences, Social Sciences, and the Humanities in the 21st Century" (Kagan 2009), which brought up to date the famous 1959 Cambridge University lecture by Charles P. Snow on "The Two Cultures and the Scientific Revolution" (Snow 1961), would deserve its own update to accommodate the expanding range of scientific cultures and reflect on what Snow termed "the gulf of mutual incomprehension-sometimes hostility and dislike, but most of all lack of understanding" that according to him characterized relationships between literary intellectuals and physical scientists (Snow 1961: 4).While Snow's seminal lecture was focused on the interrelations between the Humanities and the Natural Sciences, Kagan's book emphasised the increasing importance that Social Sciences had acquired since Snow's publication and his concern was with the "gulfs of mutual incomprehension", borrowing from Snow, that seem to separate what he terms "the Three Cultures", which by now may have already multiplied their number through new bifurcations, as illustrated later with an example of lakes research involving a range of disciplinary perspectives including some fields developed in recent decades like digital and spatial humanities.
Lakes as undisciplined objects of "x" disciplinary coordinations?

Thinking about lakes research, my closest experience, as mentioned before, was related to the longterm historical process that transformed the lacustrine environment, and indigenous cultures of the Basin of Mexico that had developed before the Spanish colonization in the fifteenth century.Although in principle my research problem was focused on relatively conjunctural issues like urban water conflicts recorded between the 1980s and 1990s, understanding the sociogenesis of the root causes of those conflicts took me back in time to the radical transformations introduced in the basin since the early seventeenth century, when the colonial authorities took the decision in 1607 to fully desiccate the lake system.This tragic project was completed only three centuries later and was inaugurated during the Mexican Revolution (1910)(1911)(1912)(1913)(1914)(1915)(1916)(1917).This epoch-making hydraulic engineering intervention not only drained the lake system but also drained much of the ancestral water cultures and lake-centred socio-spatial organization of the region's civilization.Moreover, the techno-political decision to remove the lake system also triggered physical-natural transformations that continue to haunt not just water also life in the region more generally, having placed a perpetual socioecological mortgage on the basin's population and that of other neighbouring regions that continue to pay the very high costs of a decision taken centuries ago (Castro 2006: 41-57).I often revisit this case, given its persistent relevance (Cordova 2022), and its connections with similar experiences in Mexico and elsewhere.One of these, recurrent, personal similar experiences was the encounter with Lake Chapala, Mexico's largest freshwater lake, which has been also subject to partial desiccation processes, mostly to reclaim land for agribusinesses, and has been affected by heavy pollution from industrial, rural and urban sources.In addition, Lake Chapala is still an important water source for irrigation and for urban water services in the Metropolitan Area of Guadalajara, Mexico's second city.Lake Chapala and its larger hydrogeographic basin is also the object of a substantial specialized literature (Cifuentes et al. 2011;McCulligh 2023).Along with ongoing techno-scientific and multidisciplinary studies, lake Chapala has attracted researchers working on the living lacustrine cultures that continue to resist the threat of further desiccation, urban encroachment of their ancestral territories and the extinction of life in the lake more generally.These research efforts include work on the interlinkages and contradictions between scientific knowledge and religious traditions in the face of the water crises affecting the Lake Chapala region (Gaytan Alcala 2016).Notably, one of the influential texts about Lake Chapala is a succinct cultural-historical account provided in a novel written by a militant defender of the lake (Rubin 1993).

In connection with the above references to culture and religion, their significance to the production of knowledges about water and lakes, and particularly to our better understanding of the complexities of the socioecological dimension of these knowledges, the Mexican experience provides rich examples of "water syncretism" resulting from the convergence and divergence produced by the agonistic encounters between indigenous and European water-related cultures and worldviews (Castro 2006: 56).In this regard, it is worth recalling here a contribution made by the late US sociologist William Freudenburg and colleagues with reference to an analogous, lake-connected research object, a "mountain", based on the study of the Iron Mountain ridge along the border between the states of Michigan and Wisconsin in the US, in the Great Lakes region.The authors reflected on the paradox raised by contrasting the principle that, "nothing in nature is more constant than change", and the time scales of the human experience of Nature, in this case human experiences with the mountain ridge over a few millennia, experiences largely influenced by the interactions with the Great Lakes system.The study itself focused specifically on the interactions over several decades since the arrival of European colonizers, which led to multiple, sequential, and long-lasting transformations of the cultural-symbolic representations and understandings of the "mountain", leading the authors to conclusions relevant to our discussion: while it is possible to separate the physical from the social in terms of analytical convenience, it is important to recognize that the social is inherent in what is usually seen as the physical, just as the physical is often integral to what is perceived as the social […].The larger point, however, is that what might be taken as the separably social and physical aspects of the situation were in fact at each stage conjointly constitutedconnected with one another as much as are the opposing poles of a magnet.It may be necessary, in short, to recognize or to believe in the potential for mutual contingency, or the conjoint constitution of the physical and the social before it is possible to see the ways in which the two are interrelated.Without progress in achieving such insights, however, we run the risk of having our vision distorted [… and] being prisoners of our own perspectives (Freudenburg et al. 1995: 386-88).

The authors' argument about "mutual contingency" and "conjoint constitution" of the social and the physical forms part of a long-lasting debate in the social sciences about the need to transcend the "Nature-Society dichotomy", a debate still wide open (Redclift and Benton 1994;Foster and Brett 2008;Barriere et al. 2019).It is also a diplomatic and constructive response to "realist" critics who, correctly, argue against social science reductionisms in the explanation of socioecological processes.More importantly, the proposition that "it may be necessary to believe […] before it is possible to see" how the physical and the social are interrelated (Freudenburg et al. 1995: 88) adds a closing twist to the argument that somewhat recognizes the often-blurry Vol:.( 1234567890)

space separating science and non-scientific forms of knowledge, which is also the matter of a substantial literature, including literature on the global water crisis that we face (Chamberlain 2008;Peppard 2014;Schmidt, and Peppard 2014).In this regard, there are two additional references to the production of knowledge about "lakes" that I include here to emphasize other aspects of "x" disciplinarity connected with our topic.

The first reference has close connections with the Mexican experiences considered earlier, as it corresponds to the indigenous community Lubicon Cree (Mohawk), of Lubicon Lake in the State of Alberta, Canada, who have inhabited the region since before the arrival of European colonizers.Mohawk academic women have written about the characteristics of their community's Indigenous Knowledge and the interlinkages between Indigenous Knowledge and Western science.One of them, Marlene Brant Castellano, highlighted the multiple origins of Indigenous Knowledge, that include traditional, spiritual, and empirical sources (Castellano 2000, cited in Martin-Hill 2008: 6-8).Building on this, Dawn Martin-Hill, another Mohawk scholar, argued that "Indigenous Knowledge engages a holistic paradigm that acknowledges the emotional, spiritual, physical, and mental well-being of a people, as it is attached to the language, landscapes, and cultures from which it emerges" (Martin-Hill 2008: 6-8).The author also refers to other relevant considerations about Indigenous Knowledge stressing that: Indigenous peoples assert that all knowledge flows from the same source: the relationships between a global flux that needs to be renewed, the people's kinship with the other living creatures that share the land, and the people's kinship with the spirit world.Since the ultimate source of knowledge is the changing ecosystem itself, the art and science of a specific people manifest these relationships and can be considered as manifestations of the people's knowledge (Battiste andYoungblood Henderson 2000, cited in Martin-Hill 2008: 6-8).

However, addressing the uneasy and often agonistic interrelations between Indigenous Knowledge and the dominant paradigms of Western scientific institutions in her book about the situation of the Lubicon Lake people, particularly women, including academic women like herself, Martin-Hill stated: Aboriginal people live in the shadow of colonialism; on top of this, Aboriginal women must contend with violence and sexism in their own communities as well as racism and marginalization in academic institutions.Some non-Native academics refuse to respect Indigenous Knowledge or women.What does it mean to be a Mohawk anthropologist?I still do not know.Professionally, I have been identified as the first Mohawk anthropologist in Canada.There is no home for us at universities or in academia in general.Being the first of anything is little short of a nightmare (Martin-Hill 2008: 6).
There is a wealth of international literature on similar experiences of this topic, and I come back later to some aspects of it but let us move now to the second reference.

The second reference corresponds to a dramatically contrasting experience related to the Lake District in England, which was awarded UNESCO World Heritage Site Status as a cultural landscape in 2017 given its "outstanding universal value" as an "evolving cultural landscape", which is "rooted in the vital interaction between an agro-pastoral land use system and the spectacular natural landscape of mountains, valleys, and lakes of glacial origins" (UNESCO 2017).

A recent book presents the results of a "digitally enhanced literary study" of the Lake District, a lacustrine region that not only inspired world-renowned literary movements and key authors, but also "drove some of the nineteenth century's most important advances in geological understandings of Britain's past", as well as leading examples of environmental protection institutions and practices.The researchers adopted "multidisciplinary approaches taken from literary studies, corpus linguistics, and geographical information science (GISc) to develop spatially focused, multiscalar analyses of a select corpus of Lake District literature from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries".As put by the authors in their reflection about the interrelations between the Lake District and the literary movements over three centuries, "the place infiltrated their writing, but, in turn, these authors' works have contributed profoundly toward the shaping of the place too" (Taylor and Gregory 2022: 1-3, 215).

Resuming the interrogations about water and lakes as objects of study and their correspondence with disciplines and fields of knowledge, it seems clear that the intertwining of different relevant forms of knowledge about water and lakes discussed in this section reinforces the image of labyrinthic fluidities that not necessarily converge towards a common sea of knowledge, or at least not one that is universally regarded as commonly and evenly shared or beneficial.This prompts additional problems and questions worth addressing."x" disciplinary epistemic subjects and the "scientific spirit"

Returning to the earlier discussion about the persistent "confusion" that continues to affect processes of "x" disciplinary co-ordination, it is helpful to revisit here Jean Piaget's notion of "epistemic subjects", which incarnate cognitive structures that are mostly connected to "artificially circumscribed domains", as disciplines and fields of knowledge, which, as illustrated in previous examples, may be going through different stages of interdisciplinary co-ordination (Piaget 1971: 137-139).Focusing on our field of interest in this special dossier, how could we avoid reproducing "epistemologically naïve" and "metaphysical" understandings of interdisciplinarity, borrowing from the 1972 UNESCO Report cited before (Apostel et al. 1972: 71-72)?How could we, also following alerts from the 1972 report, confront disciplinary "imperialisms", which impose artificial, though consequential, hierarchies and exclusions, mostly on grounds that are often unrelated or even in glaring contradiction with what Gaston Bachelard, writing in the late 1930s termed "the scientific spirit" (Bachelard 2002)?

These and related questions put forward in the past century retain their validity and instigate profounder reflections in the current context.As alerted in earlier debates, the problems posed by the pursuit of "full transdisciplinarity" cannot be solved either normatively or out of researchers' eagerness.In fact, as argued by Bachelard, the hardest epistemological obstacles to overcome are often the existing, accumulated knowledge and the entrenched forms of knowledge production, which may present resistance to the development of the scientific spirit, leading to inertias, and stagnation.In his words, Even allowing that a well-drilled mind may escape […] intellectual narcissism, it can certainly be said that a well-drilled mind is unfortunately a closed mind.It is a product of education.Critical moments in the growth of thought involve in fact a total reorganisation of the system of knowledge.The well-drilled mind must then be remade (Bachelard 2002: 26 italics in the original).

Bachelard's forthright provocation points at the perpetual need to reflect on the why and how scientific knowledge is produced.In perspective we must also add by whom, for what and for whom knowledge is produced.

In this connection, after several decades of longsuffering the development of our worsening global socio-ecological mega crisis, it seems that, for all its disastrous present consequences and future implications, this mega crisis may be opening new opportunities to re-examine how, why and for whom we produce knowledge about the topics that gather us in this special issue.In fact, the current crisis gives a renewed meaning to the classical forewarning stated in the mid nineteenth century by Marx and Engels:

All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned, and man is at last compelled to face with sober senses his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind (Marx et al. 2012: 77).Focusing on our topic, "water", and specifically, lakes, it seems apposite to reflect on the resonance of those words when we address the current challenges forcing humankind to "face with sober senses" our real conditions of life.

In connection with their warning, our waterrelated "real conditions of life" were appositely described by John McNeill in two chapters dedicated to the hydrosphere, which included sections on natural and artificial lakes and related processes (McNeill 2000).Tackling these global challenges facing the real conditions of life in the socio-hydrosphere with "sober senses" requires connecting the production of knowledge about water with the wider processes involving the construction of futures that may offer alternatives to the prevailing socioecological order, futures that can only be imagined as resulting from a radical reformulation of the relationships between humans and water, including our intra, inter, and trans specific water-mediated relations.

However, despite discursive preferences to adopt "x" disciplinary approaches increasingly embraced by researchers, there remains a persistent presence of disciplinary reductionisms, and determinisms that pose significant barriers to the achievement of this objective.In fact, on top of the long-standing disciplinary reductionisms, determinisms, and imperialisms that we have discussed for several decades, as addressed earlier in the article, more recently, technocentric and extremist free-market economics reductionisms and determinisms emerged as significant obstacles, not just to "x" disciplinary endeavours, with powerful and decisive impacts on the processes of knowledge production and political decision making and implementation in many fields, including research on water and Nature more generally.The production, circulation, appropriation, and uses of knowledge, as illustrated in several examples before, do not happen in a social vacuum and are permeated by human values and material interests often unconnected with scientific concerns and alien to the interests of humankind and to life in the planet more broadly (Martins 2004;Reichman 2019).A sobering example of this is the global attempt to transform water in all its forms and shapes, including lakes, into a privately owned, tradeable commodity, which in recent decades led to the emergence, among other, of "water barons" (International Consortium of Investigative Journalists 2003), which certainly also include Lake Barons.This is not a fanciful or exaggerated comment that could be avoided in a scientific article sitting along with the work of specialized limnologists.I thought that this could be the case, but then, while updating my references for this final section of the article, I came across a recent book titled "Water Capitalism.The Case for Privatizing Oceans, Rivers, Lakes, and Aquifers", whose chapter 9 discusses "Concepts of Limnological Ownership", which seemingly suggests the emergence of a new (?) side stream of limnology (Block and Nelson 2015) or, plausibly, is rather another example of disciplinary imperialism, in this case, an example of extremist free-market economics reductionism and determinism encroaching into the field of lake research.Fortunately, there are also counter examples worth highlighting, like the provocative statement that hydrology's object of study is "human happiness" made by the Spanish hydrogeologist Javier Martinez Gil, who is committed to what he calls "humanistic hydrology" (Martinez Gil 2010), in contrast with what could be termed perhaps "free market hydrology" or "the hydrology of greed", thus keeping good distance from the chrematistic instrumentality of certain traditions of water knowledge and emphasising the relevance of questions about the forms and priorities of water knowledge production.
Who decides what knowledge must be produced, by whom and for whose benefit and happiness?

Although some researchers may dismiss the significance of these considerations, often distancing themselves claiming allegiance to "value neutral science", the fact is that, as argued by Jacques Monod in his classical essay:

Ethics and knowledge are inevitably linked in and through action.Action brings knowledge and values simultaneously into play, or into question.All action signifies an ethic, serves or disserves certain values; or constitutes a choice of values, or pretends to.On the other hand, knowledge is necessarily implied in all action, while reciprocally, action is one of the two necessary sources of knowledge (Monod 1972: 174).

A succinct closing remark: The current global mega crisis of the socio-hydrosphere may provide opportunities to reorganise our knowledge systems around values and principles centred on the protection of life in the planet, which means the protection of the hydrosphere.The continued pursuit of higher levels of "x" disciplinary coordination, including relevant non-scientific forms of knowledge, remains an elusive and difficult objective, but it surely also remains an inescapable strategy to tackle the formidable challenges that we face.
